questions.question: What is a container and how is it different from a virtual machine?
questions.answer: A container is a lightweight, isolated process that packages an application with its required libraries, sharing the host OS kernel. A VM is a full software-based computer with its own Guest OS, pre-allocated hardware resources, managed by a hypervisor. Containers are smaller (MB vs GB), start in seconds vs minutes, and do not pre-allocate resources. VMs offer stronger isolation but at a significantly higher overhead cost.

questions.question: What is a Dockerfile and what key instructions does it contain?
questions.answer: A Dockerfile is a plain text blueprint that contains step-by-step instructions for building a Docker image. Key instructions: FROM (specifies the base image to start from), WORKDIR (sets working directory inside container), COPY (copies files from host into container), RUN (executes a command during image build, e.g., installing packages), CMD (specifies the default command to run when the container starts), and EXPOSE (documents which port the container listens on).

questions.question: Explain the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container.
questions.answer: A Docker image is a read-only, layered template built from a Dockerfile. It is static — like an installer or a blueprint. It contains the application code, runtime, libraries, and minimal OS files. A Docker container is what you get when you run an image — it is a live, running process based on the image. The relationship is like a class vs an object in programming: the image is the class (template), the container is the object (instance).

questions.question: What is CI/CD and why is it important in modern software development?
questions.answer: CI stands for Continuous Integration — automatically building and testing code every time a change is pushed. CD stands for Continuous Delivery or Deployment — automatically deploying tested code to target environments. CI/CD is important because it catches bugs early (within minutes rather than weeks), prevents broken code from reaching production, reduces manual effort, ensures consistent quality checks on every change, and enables teams to release software frequently and reliably.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Docker Daemon and how does it relate to the Docker CLI?
questions.answer: The Docker Daemon (dockerd) is a background service that actually performs all Docker operations — building images, running containers, managing networks and volumes. The Docker CLI is the interface through which users type commands like docker build or docker run. The CLI translates user commands and sends them to the Daemon via a REST API or Unix socket. The Daemon does all the actual work. This separation allows the CLI to be lightweight and also enables remote Docker management — your CLI can control a Daemon running on a remote server.

questions.question: What is a Pull Request and why do developers not push directly to the main branch?
questions.answer: A Pull Request (PR) is a formal request in GitHub/GitLab to merge a feature branch into the main branch. It triggers automated CI checks and requires a code review by a team lead before the merge is approved. Developers avoid pushing directly to main because the main branch represents the stable, production-ready codebase. A direct push with untested code could break the application for the entire team. Feature branches provide isolation — each developer works in their own sandbox until the code is verified.

questions.question: What is static code analysis and what does SonarQube look for?
questions.answer: Static code analysis examines source code without running it, looking for defects. SonarQube specifically looks for: bugs (logic errors), code smells (bad structure, not following conventions), security vulnerabilities (hardcoded passwords, exposed API keys, injection risks), and poor performance patterns. It generates reports that the CI pipeline and team can review. It is 'static' because unlike unit tests, it never executes the code — it only reads and analyzes it.

questions.question: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
questions.answer: Continuous Delivery means code is always in a deployable state — all automated tests pass and the artifact is ready — but the final deployment to production requires a manual approval from a human (e.g., a release manager clicking a button). Continuous Deployment goes further: if all automated checks pass, the code is deployed to production automatically with no human intervention. Most regulated or large-scale organizations prefer Continuous Delivery to maintain human oversight over production changes.

questions.question: What is a feature branch in Git and what is the branching workflow?
questions.answer: A feature branch is a separate Git branch created for developing a specific feature, bug fix, or task. It keeps work isolated from the main branch. The workflow is: create a feature branch (git checkout -b feature/name), develop and commit locally, push the branch to GitHub (git push origin feature/name), raise a Pull Request for code review, CI pipeline runs automatically, team lead reviews and approves, the branch merges into main, and the feature branch can then be deleted.

questions.question: What is a Docker registry and what is the difference between Docker Hub and Amazon ECR?
questions.answer: A Docker registry is a remote storage location for Docker images, analogous to GitHub for source code. Docker Hub is the most popular public registry — free to use, hosts millions of official images (nginx, python, ubuntu), accessible to anyone. Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is AWS's managed private registry — images are stored privately, access is controlled via IAM, and it integrates natively with AWS services like ECS and EKS for seamless deployment pipelines within AWS.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to troubleshoot a broken deployment in a cloud environment.
questions.answer: (Situation) While working on a cloud project, our application went offline after an EC2 instance was stopped by a team member, causing the public IP address to change. The frontend was configured with the old IP, so all API calls were failing. (Task) My responsibility was to identify the root cause and restore service within 30 minutes without disrupting ongoing users. (Action) I identified that the public IP had changed, allocated an Elastic IP address and associated it with the EC2 instance, then updated the application configuration files to use the new static IP. I also documented the fix as a standard operating procedure. (Result) The application was restored in under 10 minutes. We implemented Elastic IP as a mandatory standard for all project EC2 instances to prevent this from recurring.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new technology quickly for a project.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team needed to containerize a legacy Python application for deployment on AWS. I had not used Docker before and we had a two-week deadline. (Task) I was responsible for Dockerizing the application and writing the deployment pipeline. (Action) I worked through Docker's official documentation and built a test Dockerfile for a simple Python script first. I iteratively added complexity — adding the Flask dependencies, configuring the port exposure, and testing locally. I then configured the docker build and docker push steps in Jenkins. (Result) The containerized application was deployed to EC2 via Docker within 10 days. This experience made me comfortable enough to mentor another team member on Docker basics the following week.

questions.question: Describe a time you caught a bug before it reached production.
questions.answer: (Situation) During a feature branch merge, the CI pipeline flagged a failed unit test that had been passing locally on the developer's machine. (Task) As the code reviewer, I needed to investigate and resolve the issue before approving the PR. (Action) I examined the test report, identified that the test was failing because a function was returning None instead of an empty list for a specific edge case. The developer had not tested that code path locally. I left a detailed comment on the PR explaining the issue and suggesting the fix. (Result) The developer updated the code and all tests passed on the next push. The bug — which would have caused a null pointer exception in production — was caught in less than 2 hours rather than discovered by a customer.

questions.question: Tell me about a situation where you had to work with a team under a tight deadline.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team had three days to deploy a containerized microservices application for a client demonstration. We had five services and only two developers. (Task) My responsibility was to write the Dockerfiles for three of the services and configure the CI pipeline. (Action) I prioritized by starting with the simplest service first to validate the pipeline, then reused the Dockerfile pattern for the others with small modifications. I kept the team lead updated at each milestone and flagged a blocker early — the CI server lacked Docker installed. The issue was resolved in 30 minutes rather than discovered at the end. (Result) All five services were containerized and running in Docker by day two. The demonstration on day three was successful, and the client approved the project for full development.

questions.question: Describe a time you identified a security issue in a codebase.
questions.answer: (Situation) While reviewing a teammate's Dockerfile during a code review, I noticed the application's database connection string — including the password — was hardcoded directly in the Dockerfile as an ENV instruction. (Task) My responsibility was to flag the issue and suggest a secure alternative before the image was pushed to Docker Hub. (Action) I raised the concern in the PR review comments, explained that the hardcoded password would be embedded in the Docker image and visible to anyone with registry access. I suggested using Docker secrets or passing environment variables at runtime via docker run --env-file, not baking them into the image. (Result) The team adopted environment variable injection at runtime as our standard practice. This also prompted us to add SonarQube to the CI pipeline to automatically catch such issues in future.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you automated a manual process.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team was manually deploying application updates by SSH-ing into EC2, pulling the latest code, and restarting the service. This took 45 minutes and was error-prone. (Task) I proposed and was given ownership of implementing a CI/CD pipeline to automate this. (Action) I configured Jenkins with a GitHub webhook, wrote a pipeline script covering git checkout, npm build, unit tests, Docker image build, and push to ECR. The CD stage used Ansible to pull the latest image and restart the container on EC2. (Result) Deployments went from 45 minutes of manual work to under 5 minutes of fully automated execution. Human error during deployment was eliminated, and the team could release updates multiple times per day safely.

questions.question: Have you faced a situation where a process worked in one environment but failed in another?
questions.answer: (Situation) A Python application worked perfectly on the developer's Windows machine but failed on the Linux EC2 server due to a different default file path separator and a missing library version. (Task) I was asked to diagnose and permanently fix the environment inconsistency. (Action) I identified the root cause — no pinned library versions in requirements.txt and OS-specific path handling. I wrote a Dockerfile that used python:3.11-slim as the base, copied requirements.txt first, ran pip install, then copied the application code. I replaced OS path operations with Python's pathlib for cross-platform compatibility. (Result) The containerized application ran identically on the developer's machine and on EC2. We adopted Docker for all future projects to eliminate environment inconsistency entirely.

questions.question: Describe your experience with Git version control and the workflow you follow.
questions.answer: (Situation) In all cloud and development projects, I follow a structured Git branching workflow. (Task) My responsibility includes maintaining clean commit history and ensuring no untested code enters the main branch. (Action) I create feature branches for each task (git checkout -b feature/task-name), commit frequently with descriptive messages (git commit -m 'feat: add EC2 security group'), push to GitHub and raise a Pull Request, wait for CI to pass, then request review. I also regularly run git pull to stay in sync with the main branch and avoid large merge conflicts. (Result) This workflow has prevented several instances of conflicting code changes and made code reviews efficient because each PR focuses on a single feature.

questions.question: Tell me about a challenging technical problem you solved independently.
questions.answer: (Situation) A Docker container kept crashing on startup with an error: 'exec: npm not found'. The Dockerfile looked correct. (Task) I needed to debug and fix it without guidance since the senior engineer was unavailable. (Action) I ran docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh my-app to get a shell inside the container and explored the filesystem. I found that the FROM node:18 image was loading correctly, but the WORKDIR /app directory was empty — the COPY instruction was using the wrong source path. The developer was running docker build from a subdirectory rather than the project root. I updated the CI pipeline to always run docker build from the project root and added this as a note in the Dockerfile. (Result) The container started successfully and I documented the debugging process so the team could use the interactive shell technique for future Docker issues.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you improved a team process.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team had no agreed branching strategy. Developers were sometimes pushing directly to main, causing broken builds and difficult code reviews. (Task) I proposed and led the adoption of a feature branch workflow with mandatory PRs. (Action) I wrote a short internal guide covering: always create a feature branch, commit small and often, write descriptive commit messages, raise a PR with a clear description, wait for CI to pass before requesting review. I configured branch protection rules on GitHub to block direct pushes to main and require at least one approving review. (Result) Direct-to-main incidents dropped to zero. Code reviews became more focused. The CI pipeline caught three significant bugs in the first week of the new process that would previously have reached the dev server.

questions.question: Your company is migrating a monolithic application to microservices. How would you architect the container and orchestration strategy?
questions.answer: I would decompose the monolith into independently deployable services based on business capabilities — for example, authentication, product catalogue, cart, payment, and notifications. Each service would have its own Dockerfile and Docker image stored in Amazon ECR. All services would run as containers in a Kubernetes cluster on Amazon EKS. Each service would be a Kubernetes Deployment with at least 2 replicas for availability. Services would communicate via Kubernetes Services (ClusterIP for internal, LoadBalancer for external). I would use Kubernetes Namespaces to separate dev, staging, and production. The CI/CD pipeline (Jenkins or GitHub Actions) would build, test, and push images, then use kubectl to apply rolling updates, ensuring zero downtime. Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler would handle traffic spikes automatically.

questions.question: A CI pipeline is taking 45 minutes to complete. How would you optimize it?
questions.answer: I would analyze the pipeline stages to find the bottleneck. Common optimizations include: (1) Docker layer caching — order Dockerfile instructions so infrequently changed layers (base image, dependencies) come before frequently changed layers (application code), avoiding full rebuilds; (2) Parallel stages — run unit tests, static analysis, and security scans simultaneously rather than sequentially; (3) Incremental testing — only run tests for changed modules rather than the full test suite; (4) Caching dependencies — cache Maven/NPM packages between runs so they aren't re-downloaded; (5) Using faster build agents — allocate more CPU to the Jenkins build server. Combining these can typically reduce a 45-minute pipeline to under 10 minutes.

questions.question: How would you handle secrets (API keys, database passwords) in a containerized application deployed on AWS?
questions.answer: Never hardcode secrets in the Dockerfile, source code, or Docker image — doing so embeds them in every image layer and exposes them to anyone with registry access. For AWS workloads, the correct approach is: (1) AWS Secrets Manager — store secrets centrally, grant the EC2/ECS task IAM role permission to read them, and inject them as environment variables at container startup; (2) AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store — similar to Secrets Manager, suitable for non-sensitive configuration; (3) For Kubernetes on EKS — use Kubernetes Secrets (preferably backed by AWS Secrets Manager via the CSI driver); (4) For local Docker development — use a .env file passed via docker run --env-file .env, but never commit the .env file to Git. SonarQube in the CI pipeline should scan for any hardcoded credentials as a safety net.

questions.question: Explain the end-to-end flow from a developer's git push to a container running in production.
questions.answer: (1) Developer commits and pushes to their feature branch on GitHub. (2) GitHub webhook fires, notifying Jenkins. (3) Jenkins CI pipeline starts: checkout code, run Maven/NPM build to compile, run SonarQube static analysis, run JUnit/PyTest unit tests, measure code coverage. (4) If all CI checks pass, docker build creates a new Docker image tagged with the commit hash. (5) docker push uploads the image to Amazon ECR. (6) A PR is raised and reviewed; team lead approves the merge to main. (7) CI re-runs on main to verify the merge. (8) CD pipeline triggers: Terraform ensures infrastructure is provisioned correctly, Ansible or Kubernetes manifest applies the new image. (9) Kubernetes performs a rolling update — starting new pods with the new image before terminating old ones, ensuring zero downtime. (10) The new container is live in production.

questions.question: When would you choose Amazon ECS over Amazon EKS for container orchestration, and when would you choose EKS?
questions.answer: Choose Amazon ECS when: the team is small or new to containers, you want AWS-native simplicity without learning Kubernetes, you're running a straightforward containerized application with moderate complexity, or you want to use AWS Fargate for serverless containers with zero infrastructure management. ECS integrates deeply with other AWS services (ALB, CloudWatch, IAM) and has less operational overhead. Choose Amazon EKS when: you need advanced orchestration features like custom scheduling, sophisticated auto-scaling (KEDA), or complex networking policies; the team already knows Kubernetes; you want multi-cloud portability (Kubernetes is not AWS-proprietary); or you're managing dozens of microservices that need Kubernetes-native patterns like Helm charts, service meshes (Istio), or GitOps workflows. EKS has a steeper learning curve but offers greater flexibility and portability.
